claims.text: A Ti–V–Nb–Ta refractory high-entropy alloy can combine high-temperature strength with room-temperature ductility.
Conventionally processed Ti–V–Nb–Ta RHEAs contain trace oxygen and nitrogen interstitial impurities.
Ultra-high-vacuum processing, high-purity feedstock, and controlled atmospheres can minimize oxygen and nitrogen levels in the alloy.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation in Ti–V–Nb–Ta during aging at 700°C.
Aging-induced phase segregation depletes strengthening interstitial solutes from the metal matrix.
Depletion of interstitial solutes from the matrix causes progressive age softening.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will prevent or suppress impurity-driven phase segregation during high-temperature aging.
Impurity control will avoid secondary phases or precipitates that lead to softening.
Reducing interstitial impurities will preserve a homogeneous solid solution and its phase stability at high temperature.
The purified alloy will retain dislocation-based strengthening at high temperature.
The impurity-controlled alloy will retain more high-temperature yield strength than the standard-impurity baseline after aging at 700°C.
The impurity-controlled alloy will maintain yield strength close to or above 1000 MPa after aging at 700°C.
The impurity-controlled alloy will retain more work-hardening capability at high temperature than the standard baseline.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen will leave room-temperature ductility at least unchanged.
Reducing interstitial impurity levels will maintain the alloy's low density.
The standard-impurity baseline progressively softens because oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation at high temperature.
The expected improvement depends on holding alloy composition, grain size, phase fraction, and other microstructural variables constant apart from impurity levels.
Processing changes that impair densification or introduce defects could negate the benefit of impurity control.
